title: One Ångström at Kevan Shokat's Cryptic Switch-II Pocket — Shokat's 2013 GDP-KRAS G12C Switch-II Disulfide Tethering (PDB 4LUC), Sotorasib His95 Atropisomer & Y96D Escape (PDB 6OIM / 6UT0), FLAURA Osimertinib Cys797 Tether vs. Cis/Trans C797S (PDB 6JX0 / 6LUD), RB1/TP53 Small-Cell Shift & Cheryl London's Canine Mast-Cell c-KIT Exon 11 ITD Toceranib (PDB 1T46)

teenKit.tldr: Scientists can now build precision drugs that target microscopic vulnerabilities just one angstrom wide—the width of a single hydrogen atom—changing how we fight treatment-resistant cancers in both humans and animals.
teenKit.whyItMatters: By learning to lock onto these atomic door handles, modern medicine can turn previously "undruggable" genetic villains into manageable conditions, bridging human oncology and veterinary breakthroughs.
keyTakeaways: An angstrom is a hundred-millionth of a centimeter, representing the ultra-precise scale where molecular drugs must dock to disable cancer proteins.
Proteins like K-RAS were long considered "undruggable" until clever chemistry found hidden pockets—like the Switch-II pocket—to latch onto.
Cancer cells constantly try to escape treatment by mutating slightly (like the Y96D or C797S escapes), forcing pharmacologists to outsmart them with new structural designs.

vocab.meaning: A unit of measurement equal to one-tenth of a nanometer, roughly the diameter of a single hydrogen atom.
A notorious mutated cancer-causing protein that acts like a permanently stuck gas pedal for cell growth.
A molecule that can exist in different stable spatial shapes due to restricted rotation around a single bond.
The collaborative approach of sharing insights and treatments between human medicine and veterinary science.

quiz.question: What physical dimension does an angstrom represent in the context of this episode?
options: The width of a human hair
The width of a single hydrogen atom
The length of a cancer cell
The size of a tumor mass seen on an X-ray
quiz.explanation: An angstrom is vanishingly small, representing the scale of a single hydrogen atom where atomic drug design takes place.

quiz.question: Why was the K-RAS protein historically hated by cancer pharmacologists?
options: It was too large for any microscope to see
It only existed in animals, not humans
It was smooth and lacked obvious pockets for drugs to bind to, making it 'undruggable'
It changed colors whenever a medication came near it
quiz.explanation: K-RAS lacked the traditional binding grooves that scientists usually rely on, earning it a reputation as an impossible target until Shokat's discovery of the Switch-II pocket.

quiz.question: What happens when cancer cells develop a mutation like Y96D or C797S during targeted therapy?
options: The drug works twice as fast
The cancer cells change shape to cause an 'escape' from the drug's grip
The cells turn into normal healthy tissue
quiz.explanation: Mutations alter the atomic shape of the protein pocket, preventing the drug from tethering properly and allowing the cancer to escape treatment.
